parts.title: The International Meteorite Market
parts.article:
(A) At 2 a.m. on 18 July, 2011, inhabitants of the Drâa valley in southern Morocco witnessed a ball of fire streak across the sky, followed by a series of sonic booms. Scientists soon established that this was a meteorite, and what's more, that it came from Mars. Such meteorites fall to Earth extremely infrequently and the Moroccan meteorite — which was named Tissint after a village near where it landed — was particularly exciting because of the excellent condition it was in. 'It's as if it was blast[ed] off Mars yesterday,' says Dr Caroline Smith, Meteorite Curator at the Natural History Museum in London, where the largest Tissint fragment is now located. But the institution's path to purchasing the fragment embodies some of the oddities of the international meteorite market.

(B) As our sole source of non-microscopic space material, meteorites have much to teach us. 'We're still building a catalogue of everything that's out there,' says Dr Ralph P. Harvey, a geologist at Case Western Reserve University in the USA. 'Meteorite science is where biology was 200 years ago with people saying, "Oh, here's a strange, long-necked beast, I wonder if it's related to the turtle?"' Yet scientists don't necessarily get first choice of the meteorites that plummet to Earth. 'There is a market out there that treats these [meteorites] as collectibles, almost as though they were fine art,' Dr Harvey explains. The market value of meteorites began to rise in the late 1990s. Some attribute this to the advent of online businesses, which made meteorites easily available to the public. But collector Darryl Pitt, curator of the largest collection of meteorites in the world, known as the Macovich Collection, attributes it to several headline-grabbing purchases whose steep prices were unprecedented. At a New York City auction in 1998, a single slice of a meteorite sold for a record-breaking $137,000. Weeks later, another meteorite was sold for $97,000. 'Word was being disseminated throughout the world about the high prices that meteorites were attaining,' says Pitt, who put both samples up for sale. 'This served as a catalyst for a new generation of meteorite hunters.'

(C) Eric Twelker is an online meteorite retailer who purchases meteorites from dealers around the world. When asked how he determines the legality of the meteorites he purchases, Twelker pauses. 'There's some degree of concern,' he says. 'To a large extent — and I would say this is for dealers and institutions, as well — the question [of legality] isn't asked or it isn't pursued.' The law governing meteorite acquisition is diffuse. Every country has its own way of determining meteorite ownership. In Switzerland, meteorites are the property of the government — but the finder is compensated with a sum of money suitable to the value of the object. In India, Denmark, and most Australian states, meteorites must be handed over to a museum. If you stumble upon a space rock in Japan, however, finders-keepers applies. Twelker acknowledges that many meteorites are 'probably exported illegally', and that some institutions have chosen not to purchase meteorites from certain regions as a result. The Natural History Museum, for example, only purchases meteorites that have documentation giving all the relevant details. 'The institutions that have taken the so-called "principled" point of view have found themselves left in the dust by people who didn't,' says Twelker.

(D) Yet Twelker insists that the interests of science and private collection are not at odds. Collectors typically have meteorites listed publicly by the Meteoritical Society in an abstract that describes the sample's geochemical qualities and where it was found on Earth, among other characteristics. 'It's basically a label of authenticity,' says Twelker. To get listed, collectors have to give a sample to a reputable researcher, who will analyse it free of charge and submit his or her analysis to the Meteoritical Society. 'The availability of meteorites is much greater than when I started this business — and one of the reasons is that there is a major financial incentive to go out and get them,' Twelker points out.

(E) Approximately 5,000–17,000 meteorites plummet to Earth every year — some the size of a washing machine, some as small as a golf ball. But when a scientifically valuable example like Tissint lands, institutions must contend with private collectors for the prize. 'We are competing within a commercial market, although we have extremely limited finances,' says Dr Smith. 'There's a danger in the price hiking of the market. Institutions without much money to purchase things may be priced out.' The Tissint meteorite was sold to the Natural History Museum in the UK by Pitt and Dave Gheesling, another collector. 'We could have made a lot more money,' says Pitt. 'There are a lot of private collectors in Asia and the Middle East that would have paid far more.' Asked why he and Gheesling chose to sell it to the museum, Pitt answers: 'There exists a social obligation to make the extraordinary accessible. I would not have been able to sleep at night knowing that this object was in someone's private vault.' Nevertheless, the sum exceeded the museum's annual budget. Half of the money was put up by an anonymous philanthropist with a keen interest in the museum's collection. Does a reliance on deep-pocketed donors spell doom for the meteorite collections of museums and other educational institutions? Dr Smith doesn't think so: 'There are enough good guys out there who are very generous when it comes to selling stones to institutions, or providing material for free.'

Laws and requirements for meteorite acquisition
The laws concerning meteorite acquisition vary greatly. In Switzerland, the government takes all meteorites, but finders receive in return, whereas in other countries the meteorites may have to be given to a museum. To ensure they are legally acquired, one major UK institution will not buy a meteorite unless it has proper . Private collectors can have their meteorites listed by the Meteoritical Society in order to establish their authenticity. To do this, a sample must be provided and given to a researcher for . 干扰 你可能看到火星等词汇想选和科学相关的选项，但本段核心只是引出这块极其罕见的陨石及其最终归宿，并未深入探讨科学原理。

句子 Such meteorites fall to Earth extremely infrequently and the Moroccan meteorite — which was named Tissint after a village near where it landed — was particularly exciting because of the excellent condition it was in. Q15

解析 整段都在详细说明陨石价格上涨的起因（天价拍卖）以及价格上涨带来的结果（催生了新一代的陨石猎人）。

干扰 你可能看到第9句提到了艺术品就想选别的，但整段的大部分篇幅是在论述价格为何上涨及其导致的后果，选项iii概括得最精准。

句子 The market value of meteorites began to rise in the late 1990s. Some attribute this to the advent of online businesses, which made meteorites easily available to the public. 'This served as a catalyst for a new generation of meteorite hunters.'

Q16

解析 本段通过列举瑞士、印度、日本等国的不同法律，集中探讨了各国对于“陨石所有权到底归谁”的不同界定。

干扰 你可能因为段落开头提到非法出口而想找与走私相关的选项，但这只是引子，整段的核心都在比较各国对陨石归属权的不同规定。

句子 The law governing meteorite acquisition is diffuse. Every country has its own way of determining meteorite ownership. In Switzerland, meteorites are the property of the government — but the finder is compensated with a sum of money suitable to the value of the object. In India, Denmark, and most Australian states, meteorites must be handed over to a museum. If you stumble upon a space rock in Japan, however, finders-keepers applies.

Q17

解析 本段详细说明了收藏家需要将样本交给研究人员进行分析测试，以此来证明陨石的真实性并获得认证标签。

干扰 你可能看到段末提到的经济动机想选价格相关的选项，但本段最核心的内容是讲述如何通过科研测试来证明陨石是货真价实的。

句子 Collectors typically have meteorites listed publicly by the Meteoritical Society in an abstract that describes the sample's geochemical qualities and where it was found on Earth, among other characteristics. 'It's basically a label of authenticity,' says Twelker. To get listed, collectors have to give a sample to a reputable researcher, who will analyse it free of charge and submit his or her analysis to the Meteoritical Society.

Q18

解析 卖家明确表示放弃了在私人藏家那里赚更多钱的机会，出于社会责任感把陨石卖给了博物馆，即拒绝了市场高价的诱惑。

干扰 你可能看到后面提到的博物馆预算和资金短缺，会想选关于机构困境的选项，但本段叙述的核心事件是卖家主动放弃了追求最高利润。

句子 'We could have made a lot more money,' says Pitt. 'There are a lot of private collectors in Asia and the Middle East that would have paid far more.' Asked why he and Gheesling chose to sell it to the museum, Pitt answers: 'There exists a social obligation to make the extraordinary accessible. I would not have been able to sleep at night knowing that this object was in someone's private vault.'

Q19

解析 Eric Twelker 明确指出，在很大程度上，不管是经销商还是机构在买陨石时，通常都不会去追问其合法性。

干扰 你可能看到“proper authorisation”想去自然历史博物馆那段找对应，但本题问的是“不去核实合法性”的普遍现象，这正是 Twelker 提出的观点。

句子 When asked how he determines the legality of the meteorites he purchases, Twelker pauses. 'There's some degree of concern,' he says. 'To a large extent — and I would say this is for dealers and institutions, as well — the question [of legality] isn't asked or it isn't pursued.'

Q20

解析 Dr Ralph P. Harvey 直接将陨石科学比作200年前的生物学，以此说明目前人类对陨石的科学认知还非常落后。

干扰 你可能看到科学研究就想随便选个科学家的名字，但把陨石科学比作“200年前水平”的言论明确是出自 Harvey 之口。

句子 'We're still building a catalogue of everything that's out there,' says Dr Ralph P. Harvey, a geologist at Case Western Reserve University in the USA. 'Meteorite science is where biology was 200 years ago with people saying, "Oh, here's a strange, long-necked beast, I wonder if it's related to the turtle?"'

Q21

解析 面对博物馆收藏是否会走向末路的问题，Dr Caroline Smith 给出否定回答，并乐观地表示外面有很多慷慨的人愿意帮忙。

干扰 你可能觉得前文一直在讲资金困难而忽略了最后一句，但 Smith 博士在文章结尾明确表达了对机构未来能继续获取陨石的乐观态度。

句子 Does a reliance on deep-pocketed donors spell doom for the meteorite collections of museums and other educational institutions? Dr Smith doesn't think so: 'There are enough good guys out there who are very generous when it comes to selling stones to institutions, or providing material for free.'

Q22

解析 Darryl Pitt 明确表示，将非凡的物品公之于众是一种社会责任，如果只被私人藏起来他会于心不安。

干扰 你可能会把这种高尚的行为记在代表官方机构的 Smith 博士头上，但这其实是卖家 Pitt 用来解释自己为何自愿放弃高价的理由。

句子 Asked why he and Gheesling chose to sell it to the museum, Pitt answers: 'There exists a social obligation to make the extraordinary accessible. I would not have been able to sleep at night knowing that this object was in someone's private vault.'

Q23

解析 Dr Caroline Smith 明确表达了对市场价格飙升的担忧，指出资金不足的学术机构可能会因此被挤出市场。

干扰 你可能会把价格竞争带来的劣势归咎于市场卖家，但明确表达“高价会让学术机构处于劣势”这一担忧的是代表博物馆利益的 Smith 博士。

句子 'We are competing within a commercial market, although we have extremely limited finances,' says Dr Smith. 'There's a danger in the price hiking of the market. Institutions without much money to purchase things may be priced out.'

Q24

解析 原文明确提到在瑞士，虽然陨石归政府，但发现者会得到一笔资金（a sum of money）作为补偿。

干扰 你可能会根据常识自己编一个 reward 或者 compensation 填进去，但在雅思填空中，必须严格使用原文里直接出现的词“money”。

句子 In Switzerland, meteorites are the property of the government — but the finder is compensated with a sum of money suitable to the value of the object.

Q25

解析 原文明确写道，英国自然历史博物馆只购买那些附有提供相关详细信息的证明文件（documentation）的陨石。

干扰 你可能会看走眼想填 details，但结合题目中“have proper...”的语法结构，需要填的是核心名词“证明文件”，details 只是文件里的内容。

句子 The Natural History Museum, for example, only purchases meteorites that have documentation giving all the relevant details.

Q26

解析 原文说明，为了获得认证，收藏家要把样本交给研究人员进行免费测试，以此获得他或她的分析结果（analysis）。

干扰 你可能会在前半句看到 researcher 就顺手填了 Society，但题目问的是交给研究员去“换取什么”，显然是为了获取其分析结果。

句子 To get listed, collectors have to give a sample to a reputable researcher, who will analyse it free of charge and submit his or her analysis to the Meteoritical Society.
